gloss: be able, can; may; prevail over; bear, endure
summary: To be able: to have the power to do a thing, almost always with an infinitive and very often negated, “he could not”. What stands in the way may be strength, age, a law or a custom, so that “you cannot” is also “you may not” (Deu 12:17). With לְ it is to be able for someone, to prevail over him, as Jacob prevailed with the messenger (Gen 32:29; Hos 12:5) and as Jeremiah's enemies would not prevail over him (Jer 1:19); with an object it is to bear or endure a thing (Isa 1:13). Its weightiest use is the question whether a god is able to deliver: the nations' gods were not (2Ch 32:14), and Yahweh is (Dan 3:17).

words.gloss: be able, can; may; prevail over; bear, endure
words.summary: About 190 times, all in the qal (the imperfect is יוּכַל), most often with an infinitive and a negative. The infinitive construct יְכֹלֶת stands as a noun “ability” in Moses' plea, “because Yahweh was not able” (Num 14:16; Deu 9:28). Twice Jeremiah sets it beside a verb of holding in: כַּלְכֵּל (Jer 20:9) and, of the land, הָכִיל (Amo 7:10).

stems.gloss: be able, can; may; prevail over; bear, endure

senses.definition: To have the strength, skill or means to do a thing, with an infinitive; negated, to be unable, whether from weakness, age, number, the presence of Yahweh's glory, or the nature of the one who would act.

evidence.note: “The eyes of Israel were heavy from age; he was not able to see.”
“The thing is too heavy for you; לֹא־תוּכַל עֲשֹׂהוּ alone.”
“I am not able to carry you by myself.”
“How can this servant of my lord speak with my lord? … no strength remains in me.”
“If a man is able to count the dust of the earth, your seed too shall be counted.”
Their possessions were great, “and they were not able to dwell together”.
Joseph's brothers hated him “and could not speak peaceably to him”.
“The priests were not able to stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of Yahweh filled the house.”
“You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live.”
The watchmen are mute dogs, “they cannot bark”.
“Can the Cushite change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then you also can do good, who are taught to do evil.”
“You cannot serve Yahweh, for he is a holy God … he will not bear your transgressions.”
“What is bent cannot be made straight.”
“Who can make straight what he has made bent?”
“Man is not able to find out the work that is done under the sun.”
“I know that you can do all things (כֹל תּוּכָל), and no purpose of yours can be withheld.”
The fathers' doubt: “Can God (הֲיוּכַל אֵל) prepare a table in the wilderness?”
Sennacherib: “Who among all the gods of these nations was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you?”
“Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he is not able to deliver you.”
“Because Yahweh was not able (מִבִּלְתִּי יְכֹלֶת יַהְוֶה) to bring this people into the land”: the infinitive as a noun, what the nations would say.
“מִבְּלִי יְכֹלֶת יַהְוֶה to bring them into the land.”
Balaam: “Am I able to speak anything at all? The word God puts in my mouth, that I will speak.”

senses.definition: Where the bar is a law, a custom or uncleanness rather than lack of strength: “you cannot” is “you may not”.

evidence.note: “לֹא־תוּכַל to eat within your gates the tithe of your grain … but before Yahweh your God you shall eat them.”
“You may not sacrifice the passover within any of your gates.”
“You may not set over you a foreigner, who is not your brother.”
He may not make the son of the loved wife firstborn ahead of the son of the hated.
Of a brother's lost goods: “you may not hide yourself.”
“He may not send her away all his days.”
Her first husband may not take her again, “for it is an abomination before Yahweh”.
“The Egyptians could not eat bread with the Hebrews, for that is an abomination to Egypt”: a custom, not a want of strength.
“We cannot until all the flocks are gathered”: the custom of the well.
“We cannot do this thing, to give our sister to one uncircumcised.”
Men unclean by a dead body “could not keep the passover on that day”.

senses.definition: With לְ, or with no object: to be able for an opponent, to overcome him in a contest, a battle or a dispute.

evidence.note: “He saw that he did not prevail against him (לֹא יָכֹל לוֹ), and he touched the hollow of his thigh.”
“Your name shall be Israel, for you have striven (שָׂרִיתָ) with God and with men, וַתּוּכָל.”
“He strove (וַיָּשַׂר) with the messenger וַיֻּכָל; he wept and sought his favour”: the one Jacob wrestled was a messenger.
Rachel: “With wrestlings of God I have wrestled with my sister, גַּם־יָכֹלְתִּי”, and she named him Naphtali.
Caleb: “Let us go up at once and possess it, for יָכוֹל נוּכַל לָהּ.”
Balak: “Perhaps I shall prevail to strike them.”
Goliath: “If he is able to fight with me … but if I prevail against him (אוּכַל־לוֹ) and strike him.”
“See by what we may prevail against him (נוּכַל לוֹ), that we may bind him.”
Saul to David: “You shall both do great things and surely prevail (יָכֹל תּוּכָל).”
“Lest my enemy say, יְכָלְתִּיו, and my adversaries rejoice when I am moved.”
“Many a time they have afflicted me from my youth, yet they have not prevailed against me.”
“They will fight against you, וְלֹא־יוּכְלוּ לָךְ, for I am with you, says Yahweh, to deliver you.”
“You were stronger than I (חֲזַקְתַּנִי) וַתּוּכָל.”
His familiar friends: “perhaps he will be deceived, and we shall prevail against him.”
“Yahweh is with me as a mighty warrior; therefore my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail.”
Edom's allies “have deceived you, they have prevailed against you”.
“If Mordecai is of the seed of the Jews … לֹא־תוּכַל לוֹ, but you shall surely fall before him.”
Rezin and Pekah went up against Jerusalem “and could not fight against it”.
“I struck them, so that they were not able to rise.”

senses.definition: With a direct object, or with “to bear”: to be able to bear a thing, nearly always negated: what one cannot put up with any longer.

evidence.note: “New moon and sabbath, the calling of assemblies: לֹא־אוּכַל אָוֶן וַעֲצָרָה.”
“Him who has a haughty look and a proud heart, אֹתוֹ לֹא אוּכָל.”
“Yahweh could no longer bear (לָשֵׂאת) because of the evil of your doings.”
“Under four the earth cannot bear up.”
“The land is not able to contain (לְהָכִיל) all his words.”
“A burning fire shut up in my bones; I am weary of holding it in (כַּלְכֵל), וְלֹא אוּכָל.”
“Their ear is uncircumcised and they cannot listen.”

evidence.locator: Gen.32.26, יָכֹל → δύναται; Num.14.16 and Deu.9.28, יְכֹלֶת → δύνασθαι; Jer.1.19 → δύνωνται; Job.42.2 → δύνασαι; 2Ch.32.14 → ἠδύναντο, δυνήσεται; δύναμαι renders יָכֹל ×144

evidence.note: “He is able (δύναται) to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him.”
“To him who is able (τῷ δυναμένῳ) to do exceedingly abundantly above all that we ask or think.”

evidence.locator: Gen.32.29, וַתּוּכָל → δυνατός; Num.13.30, יָכוֹל → δυνατοί

evidence.note: Abraham “fully persuaded that what he had promised he was able (δυνατός ἐστιν) also to do”.
“I am persuaded that he is able (δυνατός ἐστιν) to guard what I have entrusted to him until that day.”
“How long shall I bear with you (ἀνέξομαι ὑμῶν)?”: the word the Septuagint uses at Isa 1:13.

parallels.note: “Be stronger than”: you were stronger than I and prevailed.
“Bear”: what one cannot bear, the land, the earth, Yahweh himself.
“Hold in, contain”: weary of holding in and not able; the land not able to contain his words.

phrases.gloss: prevail over, be a match for

words.summary: The Aramaic of Daniel, ten times: who is able to tell the king's dream, and whether the God of Daniel and his friends is able to deliver them.

senses.definition: To be able to do a thing, with an infinitive: the wise men cannot show the dream, Daniel's God is able to reveal it, to deliver his servants and to humble the proud.

evidence.note: “There is not a man on earth who is able to show the king's matter.”
“Wise men, enchanters, magicians, diviners are not able to show the king the secret.”
“Your God is God of gods … and a revealer of secrets, for you have been able (יְכֵלְתָּ) to reveal this secret.”
“Our God whom we serve is able (יָכִל) to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us from your hand, O king.”
“There is no other god who is able to deliver like this.”
“All the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known the interpretation, but you are able (כָּהֵל)”: יְכִל and כְּהֵל in one verse.
“Those who walk in pride he is able (יָכִל) to humble.”
“They were not able to find any occasion or fault.”
“Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God whom you serve continually been able (הַיְכִל) to deliver you from the lions?”

senses.definition: With לְ: to overcome in war.

evidence.note: “This horn made war with the saints וְיָכְלָה לְהוֹן”, until the Ancient of Days came (7:22).

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, the Targums' and Talmud's verb for “be able”, with the noun יוּכְלָא “power, ability”, which the Targum uses at Num 14:16 for יְכֹלֶת.

evidence.note: power, ability. Targ. Y. Gen. IV, 13; Targ. Num. XIV, 16.

cognates.gloss: leave (a matter) to another; (II) appoint as agent, entrust; (V) rely upon
cognates.note: Arabic w answers Hebrew y at the start of a root (as in yalad, walada), so the sounds fit; but the meaning is entrusting and relying, not being able. A shared sense “be equal to (a charge)” is argued, not shown. Named on the verb as possible: the proposal that the verb belongs with it.

evidence.note: 1 He left him to his opinion; 2 he appointed him as his commissioned agent; 5 تَوَكَّلَ عَلَيْهِ he relied upon him, confided in him.

cognates.note: Akkadian's verb of trusting, taken to come from the same *wkl as Arabic wakala. Like the Arabic, its meaning is not “be able”. Named on the verb as possible.

evidence.note: Compared there with Arabic wakala and Hebrew יָכֹל.

doctrine.statement: The verb puts the question of who is able to save. Sennacherib's servants asked which of the nations' gods “was able to deliver his people from my hand, that your God should be able to deliver you” (2Ch 32:14–15; Isa 36:14); Moses feared the nations would say Israel died in the wilderness “because Yahweh was not able” to bring them into the land he swore to give them (Num 14:16; Deu 9:28); the fathers in the wilderness asked “can God prepare a table?” (Psa 78:19–20). The answer is given in the same word: “our God whom we serve is able to deliver us” (Dan 3:17); “there is no other god who is able to deliver like this” (Dan 3:29); Daniel was brought out of the den unhurt (Dan 6:21–23); “those who walk in pride he is able to humble” (Dan 4:34); “I know that you can do all things” (Job 42:2). Abraham was “fully persuaded that what he had promised he was able also to do” (Rom 4:21), and Christ “is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him” (Heb 7:25). From the verses: to doubt that God is able to keep his promise of the land is the unbelief that kept a generation out of it; faith is to be sure that he can and will.

Of man the verb is mostly negated. “Can the Cushite change his skin, or the leopard his spots? Then you also can do good, who are taught to do evil” (Jer 13:23); “you cannot serve Yahweh, for he is a holy God” (Jos 24:19); “who can make straight what he has made bent?” (Ecc 7:13; 1:15); “man is not able to find out the work that is done under the sun” (Ecc 8:17); “you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live” (Exo 33:20). From the verses: man by himself has no power to change his own nature, to stand before God's holiness, or to fathom God's work; what he cannot do, God is able to do for him.

note: Takes j.bm.aa (the Hebrew verb) and xj.ag.aa (Daniel's Aramaic יְכִל). The brief files 34 Hebrew tokens of יוּכַל also under xj.ag.aa by spelling; they belong to the Hebrew verb, and the Aramaic word's own uses are the ten in Daniel. The names Jecoliah (j.bm.ac) and Jehucal/Jucal (e.az.ap, e.az.bp, filed by BDB under הוה) have their own name entries. Open: (1) Biblical Aramaic כְּהֵל “be able” (Dan 2:26; 4:15; 5:8, 15), and with it Ge'ez kəhla “be able”, may be the same root (a proposed *khl behind יכל); kept out of this entry until that is shown from the cognates; if it is, כְּהֵל becomes a word of this entry with root כהל. (2) The Arabic wakala and Akkadian takālu (“entrust, trust”) are recorded as possible only; no cognate yet shows “be able” outside Aramaic. Not yet consulted: CAL, Sefire and Elephantine Aramaic (ykl, khl), Dillmann and Leslau for Ge'ez kəhla, Ugaritic. (3) Jer 20:9 (כַּלְכֵּל … וְלֹא אוּכָל) and Amo 7:10 (לְהָכִיל) set the verb beside כּוּל “contain”: a hint that “be able” grew from “hold, contain”, not followed up.
